University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA Sanghyun Hong Affiliation: Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA Correspondence to: sanghyun.hong@oregonstate.edu Abstract Multi-turn interaction length is a dominant factor in the operational costs of conversational LLMs. In this work, we present a new failure mode in conversational LLMs: turn amplification , in which a model consistently prolongs multi-turn interactions without completing the underlying task. We show that an adversary can systematically exploit clarification-seeking behavior—commonly encouraged in multi-turn conversation settings—to scalably prolong interactions. Moving beyond prompt-level behaviors, we take a mechanistic perspective and identify a query-independent, universal activation subspace associated with clarification-seeking responses. Unlike prior cost-amplification attacks that rely on per-turn prompt optimization, our attack arises from conversational dynamics and persists across prompts and tasks. We show that this mechanism provides a scalable pathway to induce turn amplification: both supply-chain attacks via fine-tuning and runtime attacks through low-level parameter corruptions consistently shift models toward abstract, clarification-seeking behavior across prompts. Across multiple instruction-tuned LLMs and benchmarks, our attack substantially increases turn count while remaining compliant. We also show that existing defenses offer limited protection against this emerging class of failures. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive, multi-turn conversational settings, including customer support ( Su et al., 2025 ) , coding assistants ( Liang et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2023 ) , educational tutors ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Létourneau et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , and decision-support tools ( Gaber et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2024 ) . In such deployments, operational cost is determined not only by model size or per-token efficiency, but also by the structure of interactions between users and models. In practice, tasks often unfold across multiple back-and-forth exchanges, leading multi-turn conversations to dominate inference cost. This interaction-driven cost structure introduces new attack surfaces. Rather than compromising output quality or safety, an adversary may seek to inflate inference-time compute even with individual responses remaining benign and policy-aligned. Prior work on cost-amplification has shown that carefully crafted prompts can induce unusually long or computationally expensive responses ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2024 ) . However, such attacks rely on manipulating every prompt at inference time. In realistic deployments where adversaries lack control over user queries and defenses, output-length limiters and prompt anomaly detectors ( OWASP, ; OWASP, ; Li et al., 2025b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) are in place, existing threat model capture only a narrow subset of practical adversarial capabilities. Figure 1: Turn amplification as a conversational cost-amplification attack. (Left) Prior work amplifies cost by eliciting anomalously long single-turn responses. (Middle) Our turn-amplification attack prolongs interactions by inducing persistent clarification-seeking, while individual responses remain benign. (Right) Our approach that discovers universal activation directions for turn amplification. Threat model. We present a new cost-amplification threat against conversational LLMs: turn amplification . Rather than manipulating individual prompts, the adversary increases inference-time cost by inducing persistent multi-turn interactions that defer task completion. This threat is particularly relevant in real-world systems, where operational cost is dominated by interaction length and constrained by strict limits on latency, throughput, and resource usage. The attacker operates at the behavioral level, biasing conversational dynamics so that interactions unfold over an excessive number of turns while each response remains benign and policy-compliant. Such attacks may be introduced during fine-tuning, runtime integration, or via infrastructure-level perturbations, and crucially do not require control over inputs. Consequently, turn amplification enables scalable, hard-to-detect cost inflation that evades traditional prompt-level defenses. See Appendix B for motivating examples. Challenges. Turn amplification presents several fundamental challenges. First, turn-amplifying behaviors emerge from interaction-level dynamics that traditional single-turn benchmarks cannot capture, making it unclear how to systematically measure a model’s propensity to prolong conversations. Second, conversational LLMs are optimized to be direct and helpful ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and therefore do not reliably exhibit turn amplification by default. Standard techniques for feature discovery ( Turner et al., 2024 ) assume consistent expression of a target behavior, which limits their applicability and makes it difficult to identify turn-amplifying feature directions. Third, even if such directions can be identified, exploiting them typically requires persistent runtime intervention, raising the question of whether one-time parameter modifications can induce unconditional turn amplification. Contributions. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of adversaries that inflate the operational cost of conversational LLMs by inducing prolonged multi-turn interactions. We present turn amplification as a distinct failure mode and introduce an interaction-level auditing framework that repurposes single-turn benchmarks for multi-turn evaluation using LLM-as-a-Judge simulations. We show that turn amplification arises naturally through clarification-seeking behavior , a common conversational strategy that allows models to defer task commitment under uncertainty and sustain prolonged interactions. Adopting a mechanistic perspective, we introduce a gradient-based method for identifying a query-independent, universal activation directions associated with this behavior. To exploit this finding, we use activation steering . We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs (3B–22B parameters) across two multi-turn benchmarks and observe increases of up to 9.9 × 9.9\times in turns, 200.1 × 200.1\times in input tokens, and 6.4 × 6.4\times in output tokens. Finally, we demonstrate practical exploitation via one-time parameter modification. We show that LoRA fine-tuning with as few as 0.03% of parameters induces up to 9.2 × 9.2\times more turns, while targeted bit-flip attacks modifying only 25 weights induce up to 4.6 × 4.6\times more turns—without requiring any inference-time interventions. We also examine potential countermeasures, finding that defenses designed for single-turn anomalies do not apply to turn-amplification, and that our preliminary defenses are largely ineffective. Overall, our results reveal a previously unexplored, mechanistically grounded failure mode linking conversational dynamics, internal representations, and deployment costs. 2 Background and Related Work Conversational large language models (LLMs) generate responses conditioned on a growing multi-turn interaction history ( Dam et al., 2024 ) . In such settings, the full conversation history must be reprocessed at every turn ( Anthropic, ) . As a result, inference cost scales with interaction length rather than individual responses, making prolonged dialogues a dominant driver of operational cost in deployed systems. Despite the high cost of processing multi-turn interactions, no prior work has explored the implications of a turn amplification adversary seeking to intentionally inflate operational costs by biasing conversational dynamics. Cost-amplification attacks on LLM inference. Early work showed that inference efficiency, like accuracy, is adversarially manipulable. Hong et al. (2021) demonstrated that small input perturbations can force adaptive multi-exit architectures to traverse deeper layers, while Sponge Examples ( Shumailov et al., 2021 ) showed adversaries can drive models into high-energy execution regimes. Recent work has extended this threat to LLMs. Prompt-level attacks ( Dong et al., 2025 ; Geiping et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025b ; Coalson et al., 2023 ) craft inputs that induce long outputs, delayed termination, or unnecessary reasoning, with tools like LLMEffiChecker ( Feng et al., 2024 ) systematically identifying prompts that suppress EOS token generation. Other attacks exploit reasoning dynamics by embedding decoy subproblems ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Beyond prompt manipulation, model-integrity attacks can inflate costs globally: P-DoS ( Gao et al., 2024 ) controls termination behavior via data poisoning, while bit-flip attacks ( Yan et al., 2025 ) modify cost-critical parameters to suppress the EOS token. Despite differing attack vectors, existing works target per-turn computation —manipulating prompts or model dynamics within a single inference step. Consequently, defenses such as output-length caps ( OWASP, ; OWASP, ) , cost predictors ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) , and anomaly detectors ( Li et al., 2025b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) focus on bounding individual invocations. In contrast, our work studies a distinct axis: we inflate deployment costs by altering multi-turn interactions, inducing users to generate additional turns . Representation engineering refers to techniques for analyzing and manipulating a model’s internal activations to understand or control its behavior ( Zou et al., 2025 ) . A common approach is activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ) , which identifies steering vectors—linear directions in the residual stream—that, when added at inference time, shift a model’s output distribution. These vectors are typically derived in three steps: (1) designing contrasting stimuli or tasks (e.g., harmful vs. harmless), (2) collecting activations under these conditions, and (3) constructing linear directions in activation space that separate the resulting activation sets. Recent work has applied this approach to uncover directions mediating several behaviors, such as refusal ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) and toxicity ( Turner et al., 2024 ) . However, these applications are comparatively straightforward because the target behaviors are easy to elicit and, as a result, measure and contrast. In contrast, identifying universal feature directions for turn amplification poses a unique challenge. Unlike refusal or toxicity, conversational LLMs do not reliably exhibit turn-amplifying behaviors. This makes it difficult to collect contrastive prompts and offers no guarantee that the resulting activations encode a coherent “turn-amplifying” concept. We address these limitations with an alternative approach to discover turn-amplifying feature directions. 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework Figure 2: Overview of our framework for auditing turn-amplifying behaviors in large language models. How can we measure turn-amplifying behaviors? Turn amplification refers not merely to long interactions, but to conversations that persist beyond the point at which a user’s original query should be fully addressed. Since this work is the first to study turn amplification, we introduce a generalizable, empirical auditing framework to quantify this behavior across models and deployment scenarios. Figure 2 illustrates the execution flow, described below in detail. 3.1.1 Framework Construction Most existing LLM benchmarks focus on single-turn behavior, evaluating whether a model produces a correct response to an isolated query—e.g., answering “Nuwakot” when asked “Which city in Nepal is known as the City of Nine Hills?” ( Wei et al., 2024 ) . To study turn amplification, we repurpose these benchmarks to construct a multi-turn evaluation setting in which interactions continue until queries are deemed complete. Below, we detail each component. (1) Ground truth using LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating multi-turn interactions ideally requires real users who engage in dialogue with the model. However, conducting large-scale user studies is often impractical in academic settings. We therefore adopt a widely used alternative: the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm ( Gu et al., 2026 ) , a training-free approach commonly used for semantically complex tasks (e.g., harmful content detection ( Inan et al., 2023 ; Mazeika et al., 2024 ) and code evaluation ( Tong and Zhang, 2024 ) ). We follow a standard zero-shot setup in which the judge LLM evaluates the target model’s outputs using a single criterion: whether the original user query is fully addressed , i.e., that all aspects of the query receive a self-contained response, regardless of correctness. Concretely, after each turn, the judge LLM is prompted with the (paraphrased) question: “Did the assistant completely answer the user’s initial query?,” conditioned on the conversation history. Please refer to Appendix E.1 for the exact judge prompt. We carefully select our judge model to mitigate failure modes. We use Qwen2.5-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) due to its strong instruction-following abilities ( HuggingFace, 2024 ) and sufficient capacity to avoid inaccurate classifications. (2) Simulating user responses. To extend conversations beyond the initial turn, we use the judge LLM to generate realistic user responses to the target model’s outputs. To capture different user behaviors , we implement two response modes. In Easy mode, the simulated user cooperatively answers clarification questions, while in Hard mode, the user additionally pressures the model to provide a complete response. Please see Appendix E.1 for the detailed prompts. 3.1.2 Evaluation Protocol Each evaluation episode begins with an initial user query sampled from a single-turn QA dataset (e.g., Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) ). At each turn, the assistant generates a response conditioned on the conversation history. The judge LLM then evaluates whether the assistant has fully addressed the user’s initial query. If the judge determines that the response is complete—meaning that all aspects of the original question have been answered in a self-contained manner—the conversation terminates, and the associated metrics (§ 3.1.3 ) are recorded. Otherwise, the judge simulates a user response according to the selected response mode (§ 3.1.1 ), and the interaction proceeds to the next turn. This process repeats until the judge declares the conversation complete or a maximum number of turns is reached, which is a hyperparameter. 3.1.3 Metrics We operationalize turn amplification as the number of assistant turns required until the user’s original query is deemed complete by the judge. This captures the extent to which a model prolongs interactions beyond what is necessary to resolve the underlying task. To estimate the corresponding cost , we follow prior work ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) and record the cumulative number of input (In-Toks.) and output tokens (Out-Toks.) , which are commonly used to compute inference costs ( Anthropic, ; Google, ; OpenAI, ) . We do not consider wall-clock time, as it is deployment-dependent. For datasets that provide ground-truth outputs, such as math benchmarks ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , we additionally report the accuracy (Acc.) of the target model’s final outputs, considering only conversations deemed complete by the judge. This allows us to assess how turn-amplifying attacks affect both conversational quality and downstream task utility . 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions We ask: do universal, query-independent turn-amplifying directions exist in LLM representation spaces? To answer this, we apply activation steering ( Turner et al., 2024 ) to identify and exploit such directions. This section presents our methodology for discovering and operationalizing them. 3.2.1 Synthetic Data Generation To locate turn-amplifying directions, we require data demonstrating the behavior. As manual curation of multi-turn dialogues is infeasible at scale ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , we leverage synthetic data generation ( Nadăș et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2024 ) to produce high-fidelity conversations. We sample 5,000 prompts from Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) —a dataset consisting of diverse queries—and, for each prompt, iteratively generate a 10-turn dialogue by prompting a single LLM to alternately assume a user and assistant. We use Qwen2.5-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , which we find reliably performs both roles; alternative models are evaluated in Appendix C . The user is instructed to follow the Easy response mode (§ 3.1.1 ), while the assistant is instructed not to answer the original query and instead prolong the interaction (e.g., via clarifying questions) in a friendly, conversational manner. All responses are conditioned on the full conversation history to encourage contextual coherence. Full prompts are provided in Appendix E.2 . Let 𝒟 train = { C i } i = 1 5000 \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{5000} denote the resulting training dataset, where each conversation C i = ( u 1 , a 1 , … , u T , a T ) C_{i}=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{T},a_{T}) alternates between user queries u t u_{t} and assistant responses a t a_{t} over T T turns (here, T = 10 T=10 ). 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization We use our training data to identify latent features that induce turn-amplifying behavior.
